title: What is a multi-stage Docker build, and how does it reduce final image size (build stage with the full toolchain → copy only the artifact into a slim runtime image)?
shortTitle: Multi-Stage Docker Build and How It Reduces Final Image Size

s1_definition.profdef: A multi-stage Docker build uses multiple `FROM` instructions in one Dockerfile, each starting a new, independent build stage. An early stage uses a heavy base image containing the full build toolchain (compilers, build tools, source, and all build-time dependencies) to produce the application artifact. A later stage starts from a slim runtime base image and copies only the finished artifact from the earlier stage using `COPY --from=<stage>`. Because only the final stage becomes the image that ships, everything in the build stages, the toolchain, source, and intermediate files, is discarded, producing a small, clean runtime image that contains just what is needed to run.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India printing a batch of official cheque books. The printing workshop (the build stage) is full of heavy presses, ink drums, paper stock, and plates, all needed to produce the cheque books but useless once printing is done. You would never ship the entire workshop to the branch. Instead you take only the finished, sealed cheque books (the artifact) and send those to the branch (the slim runtime image). The workshop stays behind and is discarded from the shipment. A multi-stage build is exactly this: build in the heavy workshop, ship only the finished product in a light package.
s1_definition.oneliner: A multi-stage build compiles in a heavy toolchain stage and then copies only the finished artifact into a slim runtime stage, so the shipped image contains the app but none of the build tools.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** A multi-stage Docker build uses multiple `FROM` instructions in one Dockerfile, each starting a new, independent build stage. An early stage uses a heavy base image containing the full build toolchain (compilers, build tools, source, and all build-time dependencies) to produce the application artifact. A later stage starts from a slim runtime base image and copies only the finished artifact from the earlier stage using `COPY --from=<stage>`. Because only the final stage becomes the image that ships, everything in the build stages, the toolchain, source, and intermediate files, is discarded, producing a small, clean runtime image that contains just what is needed to run.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India printing a batch of official cheque books. The printing workshop (the build stage) is full of heavy presses, ink drums, paper stock, and plates, all needed to produce the cheque books but useless once printing is done. You would never ship the entire workshop to the branch. Instead you take only the finished, sealed cheque books (the artifact) and send those to the branch (the slim runtime image). The workshop stays behind and is discarded from the shipment. A multi-stage build is exactly this: build in the heavy workshop, ship only the finished product in a light package.

**One line to remember:** A multi-stage build compiles in a heavy toolchain stage and then copies only the finished artifact into a slim runtime stage, so the shipped image contains the app but none of the build tools.

sections.s2_technical:
A single-stage build bakes everything into one image. If you build a Java service with a `maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21` base, that image includes Maven, the full JDK, your source, downloaded dependencies, and build caches. Even after producing the JAR, all of that stays in the final image, which can be well over a gigabyte, most of it never used at runtime. It is also a larger attack surface because compilers and build tools are present in production.

A multi-stage build splits this into stages. The first stage, often named with `AS build`, uses the heavy toolchain image, copies the source and build files, and runs the build to produce the artifact, for example `mvn package` producing `app.jar`. The second stage starts from a slim runtime base, such as `eclipse-temurin:21-jre` which has only the Java runtime, not the compiler and build tools, and uses `COPY --from=build /app/target/app.jar /app.jar` to bring across only the finished JAR.

Only the last stage ships. Docker builds all stages but the resulting image is the final stage's filesystem. Everything in earlier stages, Maven, the JDK compiler, the source, the dependency download cache, is left behind and not part of the shipped image. This is the core mechanism: the heavy inputs exist only during the build, and the output image is just the runtime plus the artifact.

Layer caching still helps across stages. You order the build stage so dependency resolution happens before copying source, so that a code change does not force a re-download of dependencies. You can also have more than two stages, for example a stage to run tests, a stage to build, and a final runtime stage, and you can target a specific stage with `--target` to build just part of the pipeline.

The size and security win is substantial. A single-stage Java image might be 700 MB to over 1 GB; the multi-stage equivalent on a JRE base is often 200 to 300 MB, and on a distroless or Alpine base can be much smaller. Smaller images pull faster, start faster, cost less to store, and present a smaller attack surface because there is no compiler, package manager, or shell for an attacker to abuse.

A senior nuance is choosing the runtime base deliberately: a slim JRE image is the common choice, but distroless images (which contain only the runtime and the app, no shell or package manager) go further for security, at the cost of harder debugging since there is no shell. Another nuance is combining multi-stage with the JDK's own tooling, such as `jlink` to produce a trimmed custom runtime, or building a native image, to shrink further. A third nuance in banking is reproducibility and provenance: because the final image contains only the artifact and runtime, scanning it is cleaner and you can prove exactly what ships, which auditors appreciate.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India's transfer-service image was built single-stage and weighed over a gigabyte because it carried Maven, the full JDK, source, and the dependency cache. Pulls were slow during scaling and storage costs piled up across hundreds of image versions. This is exactly the problem a multi-stage build solves. The shipped image carries only the JRE and the JAR, dropping to a few hundred megabytes.

Problem 2 — A security scan flagged that the production image contained a compiler, a package manager, and a shell, all usable by an attacker who got a foothold. This is exactly the problem a slim runtime stage solves. The build toolchain stays in the discarded build stage, so production has a far smaller attack surface.

Problem 3 — A code-only change forced a full dependency re-download every build, making builds slow. This is exactly the problem stage ordering and caching solve. Dependencies are resolved in an earlier layer than the source copy, so a code change rebuilds only the cheap top layers.

To make this concrete we will write a Java simulation that models the build as stages. We will model a `BuildStage` that starts from a heavy toolchain base and produces an `Artifact`, a `RuntimeStage` that starts from a slim base and copies only the artifact, and compute the resulting image size for a single-stage build versus a multi-stage build so the size difference is explicit. We will also show that the final multi-stage image does not contain the toolchain. This mirrors the real `COPY --from` mechanism and the size reduction.

```
multistage-build-demo/
├── pom.xml
├── src/
│   ├── main/

│   │   │   ├── BaseImage.java              (a base image + its size)

├── Dockerfile.singlestage                   (the heavy way)
└── Dockerfile.multistage                    (the slim way)
```
sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build the simulation
mvn clean package -DskipTests
java -cp target/classes com.bank.multistage.MultiStageDemo

# Real Docker: compare the two image sizes
docker build -f Dockerfile.singlestage -t transfer:single .
docker build -f Dockerfile.multistage  -t transfer:multi  .
docker images | grep transfer      # multi is far smaller than single
```
sections.s5_journey:
The input is a heavy toolchain base (680 MB with Maven, JDK compiler, shell, and package manager) and a slim runtime base (230 MB with only the JRE), plus the source to build.

Step 1: The build stage runs on the heavy toolchain base. It compiles the source and produces the transfer-service JAR, which is only 45 MB. At this point the toolchain, source, and dependency cache all exist inside the build stage.

Step 2: For the single-stage comparison, the final image is the toolchain base plus the JAR, 680 plus 45, which is 725 MB. Everything stays, including Maven, the compiler, the shell, and the package manager, because single-stage ships whatever the build ran on.

Step 3: For the multi-stage build, the runtime stage starts from the slim 230 MB JRE base. It performs a COPY from the build stage of only the finished 45 MB JAR, nothing else.

Step 4: The final multi-stage image is the slim base plus the JAR, 230 plus 45, which is 275 MB. The log confirms the final image's tool list is only the JRE, with no build toolchain, because everything in the build stage was discarded.

Step 5: The result shows the multi-stage image saved 450 MB compared with single-stage by dropping the toolchain. Beyond size, the multi-stage image has no compiler, shell, or package manager, so its attack surface is much smaller, which is the security win alongside the size win.

```
2026-10-30 01:20:10 [INFO] === SINGLE-STAGE (everything shipped) ===
2026-10-30 01:20:10 [INFO] BUILD stage on maven:3.9-eclipse-temurin-21 (680MB, tools=[maven, jdk-compiler, shell, pkg-manager])
2026-10-30 01:20:10 [INFO]   mvn clean package -> transfer-service.jar
2026-10-30 01:20:10 [INFO] Single-stage final image = 725MB (toolchain included)
2026-10-30 01:20:10 [INFO] === MULTI-STAGE (only artifact copied to slim runtime) ===
2026-10-30 01:20:10 [INFO] RUNTIME stage on eclipse-temurin:21-jre (230MB), COPY --from=build transfer-service.jar
2026-10-30 01:20:10 [INFO] Final image contains tools=[jre] (NO build toolchain)
2026-10-30 01:20:10 [INFO] Final image size = 275MB
2026-10-30 01:20:10 [INFO] === RESULT ===
2026-10-30 01:20:10 [INFO] Saved 450MB by dropping the toolchain
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Source + pom.xml
    │
    ▼
  ┌──────────── STAGE 1: build (FROM maven:...-jdk AS build) ────────┐
  │  680MB base: maven + JDK compiler + shell + pkg-manager          │
  │  mvn package → transfer-service.jar (45MB)                        │
  └──────────────────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────┘
                             │ COPY --from=build  (ONLY the JAR)
                             ▼
  ┌──────────── STAGE 2: runtime (FROM temurin:21-jre) ──────────────┐
  │  230MB base: JRE only                                            │
  │  + transfer-service.jar (45MB)                                   │
  │  = FINAL IMAGE 275MB  (no compiler/shell/pkg-manager)            │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘
  DISCARDED: maven, JDK compiler, source, dep cache (never shipped)

  Single-stage would ship 725MB (toolchain + JAR). Multi-stage saves 450MB.
```

sections.s5d_lld:
```
  ═══ LLD — Build Stage Classes ═══

  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ─────────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Pipeline/Stages: BuildStage produces, RuntimeStage assembles    │
  │  Separation of concerns: build-time vs run-time clearly split    │
  └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ┌─ SOLID Principles Applied ────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  S: BuildStage compiles, RuntimeStage packages the final image  │
  │  O: new runtime base? swap BaseImage, no stage rewrite           │
  │  D: stages depend on BaseImage + Artifact abstractions           │
  └───────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────┘

  ── Class Diagram ──────────────────────────────────────────────

  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │        BuildStage        │ build()│        Artifact          │
  │ - toolchain: BaseImage   │───────▶│ - name, sizeMb           │
  │ + build(): Artifact      │        └───────────┬──────────────┘
  └──────────────────────────┘                    │ copied into
                                                   ▼
  ┌──────────────────────────┐        ┌──────────────────────────┐
  │       RuntimeStage       │        │        BaseImage         │
  │ - runtimeBase: BaseImage │◇──────▶│ - name, sizeMb, tools    │
  │ + assembleFinalImage(art)│        └──────────────────────────┘
  └──────────────────────────┘

  ── State Diagram: Artifact Through Stages ────────────────

  [SOURCE] → BuildStage → [ARTIFACT in build stage]
       │                        │ COPY --from=build
       │ (toolchain discarded)  ▼
       └─────────────────→ [ARTIFACT in slim runtime] = FINAL IMAGE

  ── Call Chain (Main Scenario) ─────────────────────────────

  1. build = new BuildStage(toolchain)
  2. jar = build.build()                    → 45MB artifact
  3. runtime = new RuntimeStage(slimRuntime)
  4. finalSize = runtime.assembleFinalImage(jar) → 275MB (JRE + JAR)
  5. savings = 725 - 275 = 450MB
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
A multi-stage Docker build uses several FROM instructions in one Dockerfile, each starting an independent stage. An early stage runs on a heavy base image that contains the full build toolchain, the compiler, build tool, source, and all build-time dependencies, and it produces the application artifact. A later stage starts from a slim runtime base image and copies only the finished artifact across from the earlier stage with COPY from build. Because only the final stage becomes the image that ships, everything in the build stages is discarded, so the shipped image contains the application and runtime but none of the build tools.

The reason this shrinks the image so dramatically is that a single-stage build ships whatever it built on. If I build a Java service on a Maven and JDK base, the final single-stage image keeps Maven, the full compiler, the source, and the dependency cache even though none of that is needed at runtime, which easily pushes the image past a gigabyte. The multi-stage equivalent ships only a JRE plus the JAR, which is typically a few hundred megabytes.

The win is both size and security. Smaller images pull faster, start faster, and cost less to store across hundreds of versions, and because the final image has no compiler, package manager, or shell, there is far less for an attacker to abuse if they get a foothold. I also order the build stage so dependencies are resolved before the source is copied, so a code change rebuilds only the cheap top layers instead of re-downloading everything.

On the banking project this took the transfer-service image from over a gigabyte down to a few hundred megabytes by building in a Maven and JDK stage and copying only the JAR into a slim JRE runtime stage. That made scaling faster because pulls were quicker, cut storage costs, and satisfied a security finding that the production image had been shipping a compiler and shell. The senior points I always add are that for the strongest security I go further with a distroless runtime base that has no shell at all, accepting harder debugging for a smaller attack surface, that I can combine multi-stage with jlink or a native image to shrink even more, and that because the final image contains only the artifact and runtime, scanning it is cleaner and I can prove exactly what ships, which auditors in banking always want.

---

keyPoints: Dockerfile: instructions to build an image
Multi-stage build: build in one stage, run in another — smaller image
Layer caching: order instructions for cache efficiency
COPY vs ADD: COPY is simpler and preferred
